name: Collecting Emissions Data
title: Collecting Emissions Data
answer: Collecting emissions data covers the activity data and calculated totals for greenhouse gases across an organisation's operations and value chain. It includes Scope 1 direct emissions from owned or controlled sources, Scope 2 purchased electricity, heat, steam and cooling, and Scope 3 indirect emissions from suppliers, customers, investments and product use. The work also covers the metadata that makes those numbers usable, such as facility identifiers, reporting periods, units, emission factors and estimation methods. For many teams the practical boundary is set by what can be measured, what must be estimated and what auditors will accept.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Collecting emissions data covers the activity data and calculated totals for greenhouse gases across an organisation's operations and value chain. It includes Scope 1 direct emissions from owned or controlled sources, Scope 2 purchased electricity, heat, steam and cooling, and Scope 3 indirect emissions from suppliers, customers, investments and product use. The work also covers the metadata that makes those numbers usable, such as facility identifiers, reporting periods, units, emission factors and estimation methods. For many teams the practical boundary is set by what can be measured, what must be estimated and what auditors will accept.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The collection layer usually runs on a mix of enterprise resource planning systems, utility and meter feeds, fuel purchase records, travel booking platforms, and supplier questionnaires. Cloud data warehouses and spreadsheets remain common places to stage and reconcile the data, with APIs pulling from source systems into carbon accounting platforms. Emission factor libraries and reference databases supply the conversion values, and document stores hold invoices, meter photos and contracts as evidence. Increasingly, IoT sensors and telematics devices feed operational data directly into the pipeline.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with mapping the organisational boundary and identifying which activities generate emissions. Teams then extract activity data, normalise units, apply emission factors and calculate totals for each scope and category. Estimation is common where primary data is missing, using spend based methods, industry averages or extrapolation from a sample. Controls include reconciliations, variance checks, anomaly detection and review by a second analyst. AI can help classify invoice line items, match suppliers and flag outliers, but the calculation logic and factor choices still need human ownership.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Data ownership, confidentiality and contractual rights matter when suppliers share activity data or when a company uses spend data from procurement systems. Provenance requires a clear record of where each number came from, which factor was applied, who changed it and when. Assurance providers test that trail, and weak provenance can lead to qualified opinions or restatements. Risks include greenwashing claims, regulatory penalties, privacy breaches and commercial exposure if supplier data is mishandled. Reporting rules are expanding quickly, though the specific obligations depend on jurisdiction and entity type.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Collection is moving from annual spreadsheet exercises toward more continuous, automated data flows. Satellite monitoring, smart meters, supplier portals and application programming interfaces are reducing reliance on estimates and manual entry. AI is likely to take on more of the matching, classification and anomaly detection work, while auditors and regulators push for stronger digital assurance. The direction is toward traceable, interoperable emissions data that can be reused across financial and sustainability reporting. That shift will not remove judgement, but it will change where human review is most valuable.
